summary.text: Writing \(B(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\) gives \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-B(n)\), and multiplicativity together with \(\sigma(2^{14})=32767\), \(B(2^{14})=65519\), \(\sigma(p)=p+1\), and \(B(p)=p+2\) evaluates the coprime factorization \(n=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where both odd factors are prime. The resulting value is \(2(32767)(4410)(458010)-(65519)(4411)(458011)=1\), while \(n=33085221781504\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) be the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit the counterexample
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009=33085221781504.
\]
We prove directly that \(a(N)=1\). Since this \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\), that disproves the claimed equivalence.

First reduce the divisor sum to two standard multiplicative quantities. Define
\[
B(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Because \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=\sigma(n)\), summing the definition of the deficiency gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-B(n). \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Both \(\sigma\) and \(B\) are multiplicative. Indeed, if \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, each divisor of \(rs\) is uniquely of the form \(xy\), where \(x\mid r\) and \(y\mid s\). Moreover \(x\) and \(y\) are then coprime, and the same unique factorization of divisors shows that \(\sigma(xy)=\sigma(x)\sigma(y)\). Consequently
\[
\sigma(rs)=\sigma(r)\sigma(s)
\]
and
\[
B(rs)=\sum_{x\mid r}\sum_{y\mid s}\sigma(xy)
     =\left(\sum_{x\mid r}\sigma(x)\right)
      \left(\sum_{y\mid s}\sigma(y)\right)
     =B(r)B(s). \tag{2}
\]

We next record the values of these functions on the factors of \(N\). For a prime \(p\),
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1,
\qquad
B(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2. \tag{3}
\]
For powers of \(2\),
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1. \tag{4}
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(2^k)
 &=\sum_{i=0}^k\sigma(2^i)
  =\sum_{i=0}^k(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=\bigl(2+4+\cdots+2^{k+1}\bigr)-(k+1)\\
 &=(2^{k+2}-2)-(k+1)
  =2^{k+2}-k-3. \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, at \(k=14\),
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=2^{15}-1=32767
\]
and
\[
B(2^{14})=2^{16}-17=65536-17=65519. \tag{6}
\]

For completeness, we now establish that the two odd factors \(4409\) and \(458009\) really are prime. We use the following elementary order criterion. Suppose that the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(c\) such that
\[
c^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(r\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(c^{(m-1)/r}-1,m\bigr)=1. \tag{7}
\]
Then \(m\) is prime. To see this, let \(\ell\) be any prime divisor of \(m\). The first congruence says that the multiplicative order of \(c\) modulo \(\ell\) divides \(m-1\). Condition (7) says that this order does not divide \((m-1)/r\) for any prime divisor \(r\) of \(m-1\). Hence the order contains the full power of every prime occurring in \(m-1\), and therefore the order is exactly \(m-1\). On the other hand, the order modulo the prime \(\ell\) divides \(\ell-1\). Thus \(m-1\leq \ell-1\), so \(m\leq\ell\). Since \(\ell\mid m\), this forces \(\ell=m\), proving that \(m\) is prime.

The small primes needed below are elementary. The numbers \(2,5,19\), and \(29\) are prime by trial division. Also \(229\) is prime: since \(\sqrt{229}<16\), it is enough to test the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), and none divides \(229\) (the respective nontrivial cases include \(229\equiv5\pmod7\), \(229\equiv9\pmod{11}\), and \(229\equiv8\pmod{13}\)).

We first prove that \(57251\) is prime. Its predecessor factors completely as
\[
57250=2\cdot5^3\cdot229.
\]
Repeated squaring gives the following modular calculations:
\[
2^{57250}\equiv1\pmod{57251},
\]
while
\[
2^{28625}\equiv57250,
\qquad
2^{11450}\equiv55371,
\qquad
2^{250}\equiv48088
\pmod{57251}.
\]
The three latter exponents are respectively \(57250/2\), \(57250/5\), and \(57250/229\). The required gcds are
\[
\gcd(57250-1,57251)=\gcd(57249,57251)=1,
\]
\[
\gcd(55371-1,57251)=\gcd(55370,57251)=1,
\]
and
\[
\gcd(48088-1,57251)=\gcd(48087,57251)=1.
\]
For example, the Euclidean algorithm ends in \(1\) in each case: for the second pair its successive nonzero remainders are
\[
1881,821,239,104,31,11,9,2,1,
\]
and for the third they are
\[
9164,2267,96,59,37,22,15,7,1.
\]
(The first gcd follows immediately from \(57251-57249=2\) and the oddness of \(57249\).) The order criterion therefore proves that \(57251\) is prime.

Now
\[
458009-1=458008=2^3\cdot57251.
\]
Using base \(3\), repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{458008}\equiv1\pmod{458009},
\]
\[
3^{229004}\equiv458008\pmod{458009},
\qquad
3^8\equiv6561\pmod{458009}.
\]
Here \(229004=458008/2\) and \(8=458008/57251\). Moreover,
\[
\gcd(458008-1,458009)=\gcd(458007,458009)=1
\]
because the difference is \(2\) and \(458007\) is odd, and
\[
\gcd(6561-1,458009)=\gcd(6560,458009)=1.
\]
For the latter gcd, the Euclidean algorithm has successive nonzero remainders
\[
5369,1191,605,586,19,16,3,1.
\]
The order criterion, together with the primality of \(57251\), proves that \(458009\) is prime.

Finally,
\[
4409-1=4408=2^3\cdot19\cdot29.
\]
Again with base \(3\), repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1\pmod{4409},
\]
and
\[
3^{2204}\equiv4408,
\qquad
3^{232}\equiv209,
\qquad
3^{152}\equiv3965
\pmod{4409}.
\]
The three exponents are \(4408/2\), \(4408/19\), and \(4408/29\). The associated gcds are
\[
\gcd(4408,4409)=1,
\qquad
\gcd(208,4409)=1,
\qquad
\gcd(3964,4409)=1.
\]
For the second gcd, the successive nonzero Euclidean remainders are \(41,3,2,1\); for the third they are \(445,404,41,35,6,5,1\). Thus the order criterion proves that \(4409\) is prime.

The two odd primes are distinct, and both are coprime to \(2^{14}\). We may therefore apply multiplicativity (2), together with (3) and (6), to the factorization
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009.
\]
This gives
\[
\sigma(N)
 =32767(4409+1)(458009+1)
 =32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
\]
and
\[
B(N)
 =65519(4409+2)(458009+2)
 =65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\]
Substituting these expressions into (1),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010
   -65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two integer products are
\[
2\cdot32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=132367152569400
\]
and
\[
65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=132367152569399.
\]
Their difference is exactly \(1\). Hence
\[
a(33085221781504)=a(N)=1.
\]
But \(33085221781504\neq1\) and \(33085221781504\neq12\). Therefore the implication \(a(n)=1\Rightarrow(n=1\text{ or }n=12)\), and consequently the proposed biconditional, is false.
